title: The top Latin American cities in 2026
gist: Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index ranks Buenos Aires, Santiago and Lima as Latin America's top three cities, with Human Capital the region's strength and Quality of Life (crime, inequality) its weakness. It forecasts Lima at 3.2% annual GDP growth over the next decade, plus rises for Arequipa (copper), Panama City and Georgetown (12.6% historical growth on oil), and declines for Rio de Janeiro and Cancún.

themes.theme: Index framing and Cities to Watch

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' 2026 Global Cities Index puts Latin America at the centre of its analysis, citing some of the largest ranking gains of any region versus last year and a new 'Cities to Watch' section naming Brasília, Lima, Medellín, Monterrey and Santiago as productivity-led, value-chain-climbing city economies.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The five-city watchlist is a ready-made screen for LatAm sub-national exposure (real estate, banks, consumer, infrastructure) tilted to productivity rather than commodity beta.
insights.quote: The five we covered—Brasília, Lima, Medellín, Monterrey, and Santiago—are a group of cities with diverse drivers, united by their productivity-led expansion
insights.locator: Latin American cities are at the forefront

insights.claim: Latin America is under-weighted in global city discourse despite holding about a quarter of the world's land mass and almost a tenth of its population.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Under-coverage suggests potential information and pricing gaps for investors looking at city-level opportunities.
insights.quote: Discussion of the world’s major cities often overlooks the role and dynamics of Latin America.

themes.theme: Regional rankings and Human Capital strength

insights.claim: Buenos Aires tops the regional ranking (138th overall) on the region's second-largest economy and a deep skills base from universities and corporate headquarters; Santiago is second, held back by higher housing costs and weaker Environmental scores; Lima is third on rural-urban migration, infrastructure investment and rising trade volumes.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Index leadership is driven by skills and scale, not by recent macro sentiment, so rank is a structural rather than cyclical signal.
insights.quote: Buenos Aires, the capital of Argentina, takes top spot in the region and 138th overall (Chart 1).

insights.claim: Human Capital is the region's relative strength: nine of the ten top-ranked Latin American cities also top the Human Capital score, with only Medellín breaking into that group as San José (Costa Rica) drops out.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Education and talent depth is the region's urban comparative advantage, supporting services, nearshoring and tech-adjacent investment cases.
insights.quote: nine of the 10 cities topping the overall rank for the region also top the Human Capital score
insights.locator: Major capital cities lead the index

insights.claim: São Paulo and Mexico City rank highly mainly on large GDP size and elevated Human Capital scores, i.e. scale and talent rather than liveability.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Megacity strength is scale-driven, so their relative standing depends on growth differentials, which the article says lag Lima.
insights.locator: Major capital cities lead the index

insights.claim: Quality of Life is Latin America's weakest index category because of high inequality, severe poverty and some of the world's highest crime rates, with Port-au-Prince, Guatemala City and Fortaleza cited as emblematic.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Security and inequality remain the key discount factor on LatAm urban assets despite strong talent metrics.
insights.quote: The region’s poorest-performing category is Quality of Life

insights.claim: Cutting crime alone will not lift Latin American cities up the rankings, because crime is tightly linked to poverty and inequality; the region needs broad-based interventions on the drivers of crime, meaning stronger economic performance as much as stronger law enforcement.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Policy bets on pure security crackdowns are unlikely to re-rate city scores; look for growth-and-inclusion-led improvement as the leading indicator.
insights.quote: it is much more nuanced than that

insights.claim: Lima's GDP is forecast to grow 3.2% a year over the next decade, more than double São Paulo's rate and rivalling some of the most dynamic European and Middle Eastern cities, making it the region's standout climber.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Lima is the highest-growth major LatAm city economy in the forecast; favour exposure to Peruvian urban consumption and infrastructure.
insights.quote: will average 3.2% per annum, more than double the rate of São Paulo
insights.locator: Peru’s major cities will continue their strong momentum

insights.claim: Lima is projected to overtake both São Paulo and Bogotá on average disposable income by 2050 despite sitting at only 82% and 93% of their levels today, having already passed Rio de Janeiro in 2021.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A consumer-market catch-up story: income convergence implies rising addressable spend for retail, financial services and housing in Lima.
insights.quote: Lima is projected to have higher average disposable income than both São Paulo and Bogotá by 2050

insights.claim: Arequipa, Peru's second-largest city and a leading copper producer, has averaged 5.1% annual growth over two decades with industry near two-fifths of output; a strong investment pipeline and electrification-driven copper demand should lift it into the Latin American top 10 within a decade, led by its Economic score.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Links electrification demand for copper to city-level growth; Arequipa is a derivative play on the copper cycle.
insights.quote: sustained demand for copper as electrification advances

insights.claim: Georgetown, Guyana is already Latin America's fastest-growing city economy at 12.6% average annual growth over two decades, driven by offshore oil discoveries and rising infrastructure spending; further gains are expected despite some of the highest income disparities in the index.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Oil-driven growth is real but unequal; the inequality caveat is a social and political risk to the story.
insights.quote: already Latin America’s fastest-growing city economy, with average annual growth of 12.6% over the past two decades

insights.claim: Panama City should remain among Latin America's top-performing cities and climb further, supported by deep human capital, high income per person and its position at the Pacific mouth of the Panama Canal.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Location and talent underpin a durable services and logistics hub case.

insights.claim: Rio de Janeiro is expected to lose ground over the next decade, with growth subpar and weaker than Buenos Aires and Santiago, constrained by a mature urban economy, softer demographics and limited productivity gains.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Cultural prominence does not translate into growth; be cautious on Rio-linked exposure versus peers.
insights.quote: A mature urban economy, softer demographic trends, and limited productivity gains are likely to constrain its performance.

insights.claim: Cancún's outlook is weak because the tourism reliance behind its global appeal leaves it on a less stable economic footing than more diversified city peers.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Monocultural tourism cities carry higher cyclical risk and should command a diversification discount.
insights.quote: the same tourism reliance that drives its global appeal also leaves the city with a less stable economic footing
